Widow’s Bay, a genre-bending original from Apple TV, might be the best new television comedy in years.

Apple TV is having something of a moment. In the past six months, it has launched Plur1bus, its biggest show to date and a breakout popular hit, critical favourite Margo’s Got Money Troubles, Star City, a grimly compelling spin-off of For All Mankind, and the most recent iteration of Cape Fear. With return seasons of shows such as Severance, Shrinking and Silo, it makes for enticing premium viewing.

Now add Widow’s Bay, which might be the best new television comedy in years. Rightly, last week the series was confirmed for a second season. Created by Katie Dippold, a writer on Parks and Recreation, Widow’s Bay follows Tom Loftis (played by Matthew Rhys of The Americans fame), mayor of the eponymous island off the coast of New England, as he attempts to transform the quaint and technologically backwards town into a thriving 21st-century tourist hotspot.

Standing in his way is a devilish curse: the township of Widow’s Bay is perpetually beset with terrifying calamities. In the show’s opening moments, a sinister fog descends on the island, causing a fisherman’s disappearance, as a late-night earthquake rocks the remote town.

That’s just the start of this town’s long list of odd events. Strolling through the history museum, a visiting travel journalist from The New York Times is told about how the original founders endured a famine that led them to resort to cannibalism (it took them four days), the town’s witch trials (“Great source of pride. We caught ’em. We burned ’em!”) and some of the island’s serial killers, who may still be at large (“He murdered teenage girls. You’re in your 40s, you’d be fine!”).

Is it Stranger Things meets Schitt’s Creek? Lost via American Horror Story? Twin Peaks blended with Arrested Development, with a large dose of Stephen King? The truth is, it’s all of these, and much more besides.

Widow’s Bay is untethered from the hallmarks of the modern world – patchy internet, no phone coverage and a single ferry as the route off the island – which is ironic, given the show is funded by a mobile phone and computer manufacturer. Why would anyone want to visit, let alone live, on this misbegotten island? After the journalist writes a rave review that labels it the “next Martha’s Vineyard”, tourists start to flock in. But the journalist doesn’t mention the local legend that anyone born on the island will die if they leave – a story that his research suggests may be true.

Through the following episodes, Widow’s Bay delves into a compendium of contemporary horror and genre tropes – haunted hotel rooms, zombified vengeful spirits, gothic witchcraft rituals, mysterious satanic cults and slow-moving slashers, just to name a few.

When homage and genre are so front and centre, it’s hard not to lean on comparisons. Is it Stranger Things meets Schitt’s Creek? Lost via American Horror Story? Twin Peaks blended with Arrested Development, with a large dose of Stephen King?

The truth is, it’s all of these, and much more besides. In terms of a sitcom that builds the mythology of a singular setting with an evolving storyline, perhaps it’s most like The Good Place, another show from Parks and Recreation co-creator Michael Schur. But unlike some other recent attempts at serialised genre storytelling, Widow’s Bay’s masterful tone means it avoids spiralling into pure pastiche.

It expertly balances horror and comedy, as it briskly develops its narrative. While shows such as Lost and The X-Files leant on a central tension of science versus faith, this trope is pretty quickly forgotten as the supernatural mayhem unfolds.

Mixing horror and comedy is not new, but it is increasingly popular. This year, two of the biggest box office hits have been resuscitations of horror–comedy franchises: Scream and Scary Movie. Meanwhile, Jordan Peele’s journey from sketch comedy star to hit horror filmmaker with Get Out has been followed by Zach Cregger (Barbarian and Weapons) and Curry Barker’s current box office sensation, Obsession.

Widow’s Bay isn’t Dippold’s first foray into horror–comedy mash-ups. She co-wrote the 2016 reboot of one of the most successful comedy–horror franchises, Ghostbusters. These genres both build suspense before a cathartic moment of pay-off – a killer punchline or an offbeat scare. They also often lean into exaggerated archetypes, with performances that emphasise physicality and the calculated cadence of dialogue.

Casting is central to their execution. Take out the performances of Amy Madigan from Weapons or Inde Navarrette from Obsession and those films would be limp and listless instead of terrifying and unsettling. In Widow’s Bay, beyond Rhys’s charming lead performance is a litany of incredible character actors. Stephen Root as Wyck Crawford, the old-time islander warning of supernatural doom, and Kate O’Flynn as Patricia Moyer, Loftis’s socially awkward assistant, drive much of the show, but beyond them there is a nonstop parade of “that guy” and “that girl” actors waiting to steal every scene.

It’s instructive that almost all of the homages are to film. Nailing the tricky balance between horror and comedy over 90-120 minutes is hard enough – keeping it up over the course of a 10-episode season of 40ish-minute episodes is a tightrope. Widow’s Bay walks that with a knowing sense of theatre. It’s unafraid to lean into scenes of pure slapstick and sight gags, which are spliced with sequences of pure dread and suspense.

The show’s central question is how much would you sacrifice to survive and save the people you love? While the curse of Widow’s Bay is hopefully unrelatable to most of us, its greatest success is how it grounds these stakes. The protagonists (Tom, Wyck and Patricia) are all unreliable narrators of their own stories, lying to the people close to them. And these lies are of consequence, whether or not they are well intentioned.

Tom’s eager mayor has a superficial similarity to Leslie Knope’s approach to local government duties in Parks and Recreation, but it quickly becomes clear that this is more fuelled by a desire to make the town more attractive for his son to be trapped in than it is by a noble sense of civic duty. As the season goes on, the sacrifices demanded to lift this curse become more confronting, leading to a classic “trolley problem” reckoning. And Widow’s Bay never shies away from graphic violence to show how the quirky people in this town regularly die horrible deaths.

It’s a credit to the writers’ room and a directing bench led by Hiro Murai (best known for Atlanta) that even when this balance tips too far either way, its distinctive sense of direction brings it back to an even keel.

As the United States gears up for its 250th birthday, small-town Widow’s Bay is a symbol of the originary violence of the nation’s rise to global superpower status – its crimes have not yet been concreted over. Much of the mythology of Widow’s Bay stems from the original settlers, with an entire episode devoted to both the historical hardships and systemic violence of its inhabitants.

The American horror canon was built in these claustrophobic communities – they’re where local legends, supernatural beings and ghost stories were born, before they were regurgitated as globalised entertainment. They’re places that themselves feel like myth. In Widow’s Bay, these buried histories and cultural artefacts rise from the nation’s blood-soaked subconscious, ready to sneak up and grab you when you least expect it.

Season one of  Widow’s Bay is now streaming on Apple TV.

Jacob Robinson is The Saturday Paper’s audience editor.
